label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
I had meant to tell everyone myself about the house in Glenmore. Instead, some of you heard from other people, and by the time I began making calls there were already bits of the story going round without the rest of it. That is my fault. I put off conversations I knew would be hard, and in doing that I made them harder.

So I am putting it here, on the blog Úna set up all those years ago to keep Boston and Perth and Leeds in touch with us. I would rather you all had the same account from me than another piece of it passed on over the phone.

I have agreed a sale on the house. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on **15 January 2027**. I want that date written down plainly, so nobody has to hear it from somebody else again.

The buyers are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It will be their home, not a holiday let.

I know that will not make this easy news for everyone. It is not easy news for me to write either, though I have had longer to get used to it.

The house was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. For some of you it has always been the old Mulkerrin place. For others it is Dad’s house, or Grandad’s, or simply Glenmore, with no need to explain which house you mean. It is where Tom grew up. There are people reading this who knew it before I ever set foot in it, and others whose whole knowledge of it comes from childhood visits.

I know I am not the only person with memories there. I do not want the fact that I have made this decision to sound as though I think I am.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It is forty minutes each way. That does not sound much, and for a long time I told myself it wasn’t much. I would go out, open the windows, see what needed doing and make sure everything was all right before coming home.

But there was always something else to think about afterwards. Had I checked that properly? What would happen if the weather turned? Was the damp worse, or was I only noticing it more? Even when I was back in Galway, I was still keeping an eye on the house in my head.

I am seventy-one. I am still well able to do plenty, and I do not need anyone deciding on my behalf that I should sit quietly with a rug over my knees. But I have to be honest about what I can manage, and about what I want to spend my time worrying over. I cannot go on maintaining Glenmore.

The roof survey in September brought that home in a very practical way. Ó Flaithearta’s looked at the slates and the back chimney, and the quote was €38,000. There is also the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing if the house is to be sold to anyone anyway.

I am giving you those details because they are part of the truth, not because I think a quotation for a roof settles what a family house is worth. It doesn’t. I know perfectly well that nobody remembers a summer in Glenmore by thinking fondly of the septic tank.

Still, these things have to be dealt with. They do not stop needing attention because it is painful to discuss what happens next. For a while I treated each new job as a separate thing, something to be sorted and then put behind me. I have had to admit that there will keep being jobs, and that I no longer want the responsibility of them all.

There is something else I should have told you before now.

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I told nobody. I can hear what some of you will say about that, and you will be right. At first I was embarrassed. Then I thought there was no sense worrying everyone when I had got myself up and was all right. After that, the longer I left it, the harder it seemed to bring it into an ordinary conversation.

But it frightened me. It still frightens me.

Since then I have been afraid of being alone at the house. I go out and do what needs doing, but I am conscious of being there on my own in a way I wasn’t before. I think about that step. I think about how long I might have been there if I hadn’t managed to get up.

I am not telling you now to make anyone feel guilty for not being there. You could not know something I chose not to tell you. Nor do I want a sudden arrangement where everyone feels they must take a turn minding me or checking the house. I should have spoken about the fall when it happened. I am speaking about it now because leaving it out would leave out an important part of why I have decided to sell.

There was a higher offer in the summer, from the Dublin crowd. The price I have agreed with the Joyces is fair, but it is less. I took the lower offer on purpose.

I wanted the house to be lived in. Knowing there will be two small children in it matters to me. It does not remove the sadness, and I am not pretending I have found a way to make selling it painless. But I feel better about handing it over to people who want to make their home there.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. Some of you will remember him saying it.

I have thought about that a great deal. I also know I cannot use something Tom said to answer every objection, as though he were here taking my side in an argument. He isn’t here. That is the difficulty underneath all the other difficulties. I have had to make this decision without him, and I would have given a great deal not to have to.

When I think of Glenmore, I still think of him there. I expect I always will.

He proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were watching. I have never felt the need to improve that story. There was no beautiful sunset, and I was not wearing anything worth describing. There was Tom, asking me, and there was myself saying yes, with an audience neither of us had invited.

I cannot stand behind the house without remembering it.

Then there were the children learning to swim in the lake below, and the business of getting them out again afterwards. Declan would refuse to come out until his lips were blue. You could tell him he was frozen and he would deny it with his teeth going. I wonder how many hours altogether we spent standing there telling children that yes, they had had long enough.

Those are the things that come back to me. Not a tidy account of the house or one grand occasion, but a wet day, a voice, somebody refusing to do what they were told. I know each of you will have your own things. I hope you will keep telling them, including the ones I have forgotten or never knew.

Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I did not feel that clearly at the beginning. There were times when even thinking about selling seemed disloyal. I would go out to check the pipes and find myself feeling that I ought to be doing more, though I could not have said what more would have been.

I miss Tom. Keeping the house has not made me miss him less. Selling it will not mean that I have finished missing him.

I want to say something about Declan, because I have already said enough badly in private, and I do not want anyone supplying their own version of what happened.

Declan heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp. He should have heard it from me. Whatever else we disagree about, there is no getting round that.

He rang me at two in the morning his time. He was very upset. He said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back that I should not have said.

I am not going to repeat the rest of our conversation here. It was between the two of us, and putting it on the blog would not improve it. But I do need to acknowledge my part in it. I knew this would hurt him, and instead of speaking to him properly before agreeing the sale, I delayed. Then, when he rang hurt and angry, I did not respond as I wish I had.

Declan, I am sorry you found out that way. I am sorry I did not consult you before I agreed the sale, and I am sorry for the things I said on the phone.

I can understand that the house feels like part of your dad. It feels like part of him to me too. I should have given you the chance to speak to me about it before it reached this point, even knowing that we might not agree.

But I am not sorry for deciding to sell, and I do not want to give you a false impression about that. I am not willing to wait until your summer visit. The sale closes on 15 January, and I intend to go ahead with it.

I know that is hard to read. I have gone over it many times, including whether I could manage a little longer. I do not want to keep saying I can when the truth is that I cannot go on with it.

I am not angry with you. You do not have to come round to my way of thinking before we can speak again. You can still be upset with me, and I can still want to hear from you. The door is open. I love you, and I do not want our last conversation about this to be the one we had in the middle of your night.

For everyone wondering what will happen to the things in the house, there are some things I can tell you now.

We are keeping the dresser. It is going to Úna’s. We are keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign.

I know those things will mean different amounts to different people, but I wanted you to know they are not being left behind in the clearing of the house. There will be plenty to sort, and I am sure there will be things I need reminding about. Please speak to me directly if there is something you are worried about. I would much rather have the conversation than discover afterwards that somebody was distressed and said nothing.

The Joyces have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. That was kind of them, and I am grateful.

Of course, it will be their home, and we will have to respect that. We cannot go on treating the place exactly as we did when Tom was alive. But it is a comfort to know that selling does not have to mean never walking there again.

Before the house is cleared, I would like us to have a day there together.

**Sunday 13 December** is the day. Anyone who can come is welcome. There will be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies.

I know December is awkward, especially for those of you a long way away. This is not a summons, and nobody needs to explain the cost of flights or time off work to me. I would love to see whoever can make it. If you cannot, I hope you will send a memory or a photograph, or give us a ring.

There is no programme for the day. We can have something to eat, walk out if the weather allows it, and spend some time in the house before it is cleared. I would like to hear the stories people remember, particularly the ones that will make us laugh. Tom was a real person, with faults and notions of his own, and there is no need to turn him into a saint because we miss him.

There is no need for everyone to arrive cheerful either. I expect it will be a strange day. We can let it be that without trying to make it into either a celebration or a funeral.

I have spent a long time wondering whether there was a way to do this that would leave nobody hurt. There isn’t, but that does not excuse the way I let the news get out. You deserved to hear it properly from me. I am sorry that some of you didn’t.

I hope this at least gives everyone the full account: why I am selling, what is being kept, who is buying the house and when it will happen. You may still disagree with me. I would rather you disagreed with what I have actually said than with something that has travelled through three phone calls.

The sale closes on **15 January 2027**. Before then, I hope as many of us as possible will be together in Glenmore on **Sunday 13 December**.

Let me know if you can come, so I have some idea how much soup to make. And do bring the wellies.
